No developer knowledge is necessary.' So read option C as naming a supported implementation, not an unavoidable prerequisite; a modern build can satisfy this requirement declaratively.
findings.note: Key A,C left in place but the item is now partly stale, and the explanation says so instead of asserting the old absolute. Option C claims 'Apex coding skills are needed for the Registration Handler', which was true when the item was written and is no longer: Salesforce documents Flow Builder as a first-class registration handler type requiring no developer knowledge. That also makes option B closer to true than the deck allowed. I did not move the key to A,B because B's wording names Process Builder, which is retired, so neither option is cleanly correct as printed. Flagged as a judgement call for the user: the cleanest repair is to reword C to 'a registration handler is required (Apex or Flow)' rather than to reletter the key.

Key A confirmed against the documented personalisation mechanism. Audience targeting is described as assembling 'a set of criteria that defines a user segment' so you can 'tailor a single site to meet the needs of multiple user segments... present the same site with a different look and feel for each audience or show different pages, components, or data to different audiences', with criteria types that are 'user related or record related'. That is precisely storing what the customer supplied at registration on the User and Contact records and letting the pages vary on it — one site, many experiences. The alternatives all multiply artefacts to achieve the same thing: different profiles (B) and custom permissions (C) are access-control mechanisms being borrowed for presentation, and separate login flows per persona (D) branch the login process rather than the experience. One caveat this item should not be read against: the same page warns that 'an audience varies what your site visitors can see, but don't use audiences to keep sensitive data private. Instead, use standard security methods.' Audience targeting is presentation, not security.

Key A,B confirmed, each from its own documented instruction. A comes from the connected app OAuth policies page, which prescribes this configuration outright for a signed-request canvas app: 'Set Permitted Users to Admin-approved users are pre-authorized. Set Expire Refresh Tokens to Immediately expire refresh token.' Pre-authorisation is what removes the per-user approval prompt and lets admins decide which agents get the app. B comes from the Canvas guide: 'SAML SSO enables you to give your users automatic authentication into your canvas app via SAML and authentication into Salesforce via the signed request', and 'you can create a canvas app that begins a standard SAML authentication flow when opened by a user' — begun by the app, i.e. service-provider initiated. That direction is also the only one available, since Identity Provider Initiated is documented as unsupported for canvas apps on communities. C would reintroduce a user authorisation step, and D makes it a personal app, taking the choice away from admins.

Key A,B confirmed, with the item turning on Salesforce holding two roles at once in two different protocols. B follows from the documented definition: 'The system that authenticates users is called an identity provider. The system that trusts the identity provider for authentication is called the service provider' — Okta authenticates and Salesforce trusts it, so Salesforce is the SAML service provider, which also rules out C. A follows from the OAuth side: tokens 'authorize access to protected resources', and here the protected resources are Salesforce records that the Forecasting app calls on the user's behalf, so Salesforce is the party hosting and protecting them while the Forecasting app is the client, ruling out D. Stated precisely: 'resource server' is standard OAuth terminology rather than a phrase quoted from these two pages, so A rests on the documented role of Salesforce as the holder of the protected resources.

Key B confirmed, and Salesforce has a documented name for this topology: an identity provider chain. 'If you want users to log in to Salesforce from a third-party identity provider and immediately have access to a client app, set up an identity provider chain.' That is the stem — PingFederate authenticates users into the Salesforce org, and that org in turn asserts identity to the financial and CPQ systems, so PingFederate and Org1 are both acting as identity providers while Org1 is simultaneously a service provider to PingFederate. The distractors each collapse one half of the chain: A and C name only service providers and so omit Org1's IdP role, and D promotes Org2 to an IdP when nothing in the scenario has it asserting identity to anything.

Key A,C confirmed from the same article that settles the other Salesforce-as-IdP items in this deck. C is the registration step: an external app is integrated by configuring it as a connected app with the Salesforce org defined as its SAML identity provider. A is documented in one sentence — 'Specifying a Start URL makes the application available in the app menu and in App Launcher' — which is how portal users reach the third-party app with SSO already established. B is the wrong direction: Delegated Authentication has Salesforce call out to an external service to validate credentials, making Salesforce the consumer of authentication rather than the provider, which contradicts the stem's premise. D is not an identity feature at all — an External Data Source with a Named Principal surfaces external *data* under a single shared credential and provides no per-user login to the third-party app.

Key D confirmed, and the reference guide's own worked example is nearly this scenario: it 'authorizes the connected app user to use the connected app if the context is SAML and the user has reached the quota tracked in a custom field.' Swap the quota for an open Classified case and that is the requirement exactly — a decision taken per SSO attempt, in a SAML context, from live record data. The class is described as the way 'to customize how the app is invoked... respond to user attributes in a way that benefits a business process', and 'when you use the authorize method, the execution user authorizes the connected app to access data'. The rejected options all evaluate at the wrong moment: JIT (A) runs at user creation or update on login rather than querying live case ownership as an access gate, an Apex trigger granting and revoking permission sets (B) leaves access standing between case events and adds mixed-DML fragility, and a report (C) is not an enforcement mechanism at all.

Key D confirmed, and the two requirements split cleanly across the two protocols. SCIM covers the lifecycle half: 'You can provision and manage your Salesforce user identities across systems with the open standard System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM)', and you 'send REST API create, read, update, and disable (CRUD) operations to SCIM endpoints' — a push from the central IAM the moment a status changes, which is requirement 1. SAML with Salesforce as service provider covers requirement 2. The decisive argument against B is a timing one: JIT provisioning creates or updates a user 'the first time a user logs in with a SAML identity provider', so it only ever runs on a login, and a user disabled centrally never logs in again and is therefore never deactivated. A fails for the same reason. C is ruled out by scope, since Identity Connect integrates Microsoft Active Directory rather than a cloud IAM service.

Key A,B,C confirmed, all three from the User Provisioning article. B and A are the setup pair — you configure user provisioning for a connected app representing the third-party system, exactly as the article's own G Suite example does. C is settled by two specifics on that page: 'The operation value is stored in the UserProvisioningRequest object', and 'Salesforce can either process the request immediately or wait for an approval process to complete (if you requested approvals when running the wizard).' So the approval gate belongs on the standard UserProvisioningRequest object that the framework already generates, which is what makes accounts appear in Concur only after sign-off. That is also why D and E are wrong: a custom object (D) is unnecessary because the standard object exists for this purpose, and the User object (E) is the wrong target, since provisioning requests rather than user records are what await approval.

Key A confirmed by the field's own definition. When an identity provider registers a service provider, the value it stores is 'Entity Id—The globally unique ID of the service provider.' Globally unique is the whole point of the question: it is what lets the IdP tell this Salesforce org apart from every other service provider it serves, and why two orgs federating to one IdP need distinct Entity Ids. The distractors are all real SAML SSO fields pointing the other way or at another party: Issuer (B) identifies the *identity* provider rather than Salesforce; SAML Identity Location (C) says where in the assertion the user identifier sits (Subject versus an attribute element); and Identity Provider Login URL (D) is the endpoint Salesforce sends its AuthnRequest to. None of them identifies Salesforce to the IdP.

Key B confirmed by the FAQ's answer to 'Are there any requirements for implementing my web service?': 'For security reasons, make your web service available by TLS. A certificate from a trusted provider, such as Verisign or Thawte, is required. For a list of trusted providers, contact Salesforce.' The same answer adds that the service belongs on a server in your DMZ, reachable at an external DNS name. Option A is refuted a few lines later, where the mapping guidance is to 'Map your org's internal usernames to your Salesforce usernames' — delegated authentication keys on username, while Federation ID is a SAML SSO field. C invents a parameter range, and D is unnecessary because TLS protects the credentials in transit; the service validates them rather than decrypting a Salesforce-encrypted payload. Citation note for future passes: this requirement is on the FAQs article, not on 'Configure Salesforce for Delegated Authentication', which never mentions TLS.

Key B confirmed, and the article draws the exact line the item tests: 'OAuth tokens authorize access to protected resources... Scopes further define the type of protected resources that the connected app can access. You assign scopes to a connected app when you build it, and they're included with the OAuth tokens during the authorization flow.' So the access token (A) is what grants access while the scope is what bounds which resources — restricting resource types is the scope's job, which is why A is the near-miss rather than a wrong-sounding option. Refresh tokens (D) govern session longevity, not resource reach, and 'Mobile PINs' (C) relate to device-level app protection and do not scope API access.

Key A confirmed, with the admin-authorization requirement in the stem being the discriminator. The article is titled 'OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow for Previously Authorized Apps' and states that 'a client—via a connected app—can use previous authorization by supplying a signed SAML 2.0 assertion to request an OAuth access token', where the token endpoint 'issues an access_token based on prior approval of the app'. Prior approval via a connected app is exactly the administrator authorisation the stem requires. Option B is a genuine trap rather than a nonsense answer, because Salesforce does document a separate SAML Assertion Flow; the difference is that the bearer assertion flow runs through a connected app and its pre-approval, which is what the requirement names. C is an interactive browser flow unsuited to API consumers, and D authenticates with a JWT rather than SAML.

Key D confirmed by a sentence that matches the option almost word for word: 'When deprovisioned, the user's Salesforce session is revoked immediately.' The same page kills the other three. B is wrong on deployment — 'Identity Connect runs as a service on either Windows or Linux platforms' and 'is installed on a server', so it is not a managed package and gains nothing from platform high availability. C is wrong on role: Identity Connect synchronises AD accounts into Salesforce user records and can be used for SSO to Salesforce; it is not an identity provider to Active Directory. A describes FIFO license-based deactivation, which appears nowhere in the documentation. Housekeeping note: this question's id also appears in the deleted findings-integration-architect.json, which explains why its explanation had already been improved without any correction stamp on the question.

Key A confirmed. The stem's three requirements are provision, deprovision, and authenticate against an existing Microsoft AD, and the article covers all three in order: 'Identity Connect integrates Microsoft Active Directory (AD) user accounts with Salesforce user records... when a user is created in AD, the Salesforce user record is created as part of the provisioning process. When deprovisioned, the user's Salesforce session is revoked immediately. You can also use Identity Connect for single sign-on to Salesforce.' That is a product doing the job, which rules out B's custom integration. C is wrong because AD alone does not maintain Salesforce user records, and D overstates what the base licenses include: the page states Identity Connect is 'available for an additional cost in Enterprise, Performance, and Unlimited Editions', so it does need separate consideration.

Key A confirmed on the product's scope rather than by elimination. The article's opening sentence defines Identity Connect entirely in terms of one directory — 'Identity Connect integrates Microsoft Active Directory (AD) user accounts with Salesforce user records' — and no other identity store is mentioned anywhere on the page. UC keeps its corporate identities in a custom database, so the product simply does not apply, which is the limitation the IT manager needs to hear. That also disposes of B, C and D: each presupposes Identity Connect working in this environment and merely disagrees about which SAML flow or feature is available, when the real answer is that it is not a candidate at all.

Key B confirmed, same documented sentence that settles the near-identical item earlier in the deck: 'Purchase the Identity Only license when you need extra licenses for employees to access only identity services, such as single sign-on (SSO)', illustrated with employees who do not need the full Salesforce feature set but must sign in to a custom web app from their org. That is this stem exactly — employees, no object access, a custom Benefits app, Salesforce credentials. External Identity (A) is scoped by the same page to Experience Cloud users who are 'consumers of your business, such as customers, prospective customers, patients, partners, and dealers', so it is the wrong side of the employee/external divide. C is an SMS add-on, and D is an AD-integration product, neither of them access licenses.

Key A,C confirmed on both halves. A: the External Identity license carries Salesforce Customer Identity and 'applies to Experience Cloud users who don't already have a community license... typically consumers of your business', which is the CIAM population in the stem, and authentication-only is exactly its scope. C: a mobile-first design that accepts a phone number as username delivers one-time passcodes by SMS, and the add-on licence is denominated in SMS sends — 'typically includes 25,000 SMS messages per month'. Option D is the item's sharpest distractor because it sounds symmetrical but does not exist: there is no Email Verification Credits license, since email delivery of a passcode consumes no credits. Identity Connect (B) synchronises Active Directory for employees and has no role in external CIAM.

Key A confirmed. The customers here authenticate through external auth providers and SSO out to an off-platform app via OAuth, with no requirement for Experience Cloud record features — which matches the External Identity license, documented as carrying Salesforce Customer Identity for 'consumers of your business, such as customers, prospective customers, patients, partners, and dealers'. The same page positions the alternative explicitly: 'You can upgrade the External Identity license to a Community license to benefit from Experience Cloud features, including Cases, Contracts, Notes, Orders, and Tasks' — none of which this stem needs, which is what rules out C and D. Identity Only (B) is the employee-side license, so it is the wrong population.

Key C confirmed. 'To integrate IoT devices with the Salesforce API, use the OAuth 2.0 asset token flow', and asset tokens 'allow registration of device data with the Salesforce platform and linking the device to Salesforce CRM data' — a fleet of Wi-Fi GPS trackers posting coordinates is that case, and per-device tokens give each container a revocable identity. Worth noting the stem's 'no direct user input or output capabilities' reads like the device flow trigger phrase, but the device flow is not among the options and would be wrong anyway: it requires a human to enter a user code at a verification URL in a browser, which unattended shipping containers cannot do. Of the options offered, JWT Bearer (B) is a server-to-server pattern with no device identity, and username-password (D) is the flow Salesforce is retiring.

Key B,D confirmed. This is the option-shuffled variant of the self-registration item earlier in the deck and resolves to the same two mechanisms, so the pair is internally consistent: 'Next to CommunitiesSelfReg, click Edit' for the custom Visualforce page that captures the extra data elements, and 'For more control over the self-registration process, edit the CommmunitiesSelfRegController' (Salesforce's own three-m spelling) for the profile and account assignment logic. Option C remains invented — there is no SelfRegistration trigger. Option A is the same near-miss as in the sibling question: the controller is edited, but the thing you configure in Login & Registration is the page.

Key D confirmed. The registration handler article describes the returning-user path in exactly these terms: 'If there is a matching user, the registration handler updates the user record with information from the identity provider', and lists among the handler's minimum tasks 'Update an existing user with information from the identity provider'. Since the handler runs on every authentication through the auth provider, that update path is what keeps a changing Facebook profile in sync, and the Apex method carrying it is updateUser(). Option B crosses the documented pairings — Facebook is an Auth Provider integration, and JIT provisioning belongs to SAML. Option C mistakes Canvas signed requests for auth provider callbacks. Option A would work only nightly and duplicates a mechanism the platform already runs at login.

Key B confirmed — this is the option-shuffled variant of the question at #37 and resolves to the same mechanism, updateUser() on the registration handler, so the two are consistent with each other. Documented in the same sentence: 'If there is a matching user, the registration handler updates the user record with information from the identity provider.' Recorded deliberately rather than skipped as a duplicate: the deck's structural audit flags this stem as colliding with another, and confirming both variants keep the same answer is what makes that collision benign rather than a defect.

Key B confirmed, and the documentation describes the association as the handler's defining job: among its minimum tasks are 'Take information from the identity provider and look for a matching user record in Salesforce' and 'Decide whether to create a user or update an existing user.' The Mobile SDK guide shows the concrete form — filter on 'any unique data in the Facebook packet, such as username or email address, and then validate that data against similar fields in your Experience Cloud site members' records.' That is precisely associating a Facebook user with a Salesforce user. Consumer Key and Secret (A) authenticate Salesforce to Facebook, not one user to another; the User Info Endpoint (C) supplies the attributes the handler then matches on; a Federation ID (D) is a SAML SSO field, not part of the auth provider framework.

Key D confirmed. First-login provisioning is the handler's create path — 'the registration handler creates a user record' when no match is found, and 'Create a complete user record based on information from the identity provider' is one of its minimum tasks — so createUser() is the hook that fires exactly once per new customer, which is what the stem asks for. Apex is the correct handler type here rather than Flow, since the article's own comparison notes Apex 'supports more complex use cases', and an outbound callout to the accounting web service is such a case. Option B misapplies JIT, which is SAML-side and provisions users into Salesforce rather than into a third-party system; C describes a token flow, not a trigger point; A adds a Heroku app to do what the handler already does in-platform.

Key A,B,D confirmed, and the three map onto the documented setup sequence. A: Authentication Provider SSO states that with auth providers 'your users can log in to your Salesforce org or Experience Cloud site with single sign-on (SSO) using credentials from a third party', and Salesforce ships provider types for both Facebook and LinkedIn. B: the Auth Provider documentation set includes a dedicated step for adding an authentication provider to an Experience Cloud site's login page, which is where the social buttons are switched on. D: 'To set up single sign-on (SSO) with an authentication provider, you must set up a registration handler' — the handler is mandatory, not optional, and the auto-created class must be updated to create and update users. E is the standard inversion: a Connected App makes Salesforce the identity provider to an external app, the opposite direction from social sign-on. C belongs to SAML federation, not the auth provider framework.

Key B,C confirmed against the threats Salesforce itself names: 'To protect users from security threats like phishing, credential stuffing, and account takeovers, Salesforce requires MFA for all logins to Salesforce products.' Both keyed options are instances of those. Credentials captured on a public Wi-Fi access point (B) are stolen credentials, and MFA's defining property — 'a second piece of evidence (or factor) in addition to their password' — is what makes them insufficient. A password shared with Facebook (C) is the credential-stuffing case exactly: a breach elsewhere yields a working password that still fails without the second factor. The rejected pair fails on timing and scope: an unattended, already-authenticated laptop (D) is a live session, and MFA acts at login, so session timeout and screen lock are the controls there; weak password-reset questions (A) are a password-policy matter, not a second-factor one.

Key B,C confirmed, with B documented and C a short step from the same sentences. The Single Sign-On article defines the capability as 'an authentication method that enables users to access multiple applications with one login and one set of credentials', and names the role: 'The system that authenticates users is called an identity provider.' Authenticating many applications is therefore the IdP's defining function, which is B. C follows from 'one set of credentials' — consolidating credentials into the IdP is what makes one password policy enforceable everywhere, though stated plainly, the article does not use the phrase 'password policy', so C rests on that inference rather than a quotable line. A is the real distractor and is wrong on mechanism: an IdP holds a single credential set and issues assertions or tokens to each service provider; it does not store per-application credentials, which is what a password vault does. D describes a CIAM use case rather than the enterprise business case the stem asks for.

Key B confirmed as the option that satisfies all four requirements with the least build. SSO is defined as configuring 'one system to trust another to authenticate users, eliminating the need for users to log in to each system separately', and a Salesforce org can act as the SAML identity provider for other service providers — org-to-org federation is a supported configuration, not custom development. That keeps the existing multi-org, multi-country footprint (requirement 2), gives each partner a home org (3), and delivers one login across the community orgs (4). The alternatives all cost more: C consolidates every country into a single org, which is a re-architecture rather than a configuration; A replaces SSO with bespoke API work; D makes the user choose an org per session and still needs login flows to route them. Judgement call flagged: this item is an architecture-preference question rather than one a single documentation sentence settles, so B is the best-supported answer rather than a documented absolute.

Key A confirmed, and the stem's odd-looking detail about the team being willing to add JavaScript is exactly what selects it. The Canvas Developer Guide describes Canvas as 'a set of tools and JavaScript APIs that you can use to expose an application as a Canvas app', and lists among those tools 'Authentication—If your application requires authorization, you can implement it by using a signed request or OAuth 2.0.' So signed request is a documented Canvas authentication method and Canvas is what requires the JS additions UC consented to. App Launcher (B) would launch the app but not carry identity into it, a user-agent Connected App (C) would still prompt for authorisation, and rewriting in Visualforce (D) discards the existing app. Currency flag for a future pass: the same page warns that Canvas apps are affected by third-party cookie restrictions, so this is a mechanism under browser pressure even though it remains documented.

Key A,B confirmed, both named in the documentation. Modify the Default Self-Registration Page instructs you to find Visualforce Pages, 'Next to CommunitiesSelfReg, click Edit' and add code to customise the fields collected — that is the custom Visualforce page in option B, and it is where the extra data elements are captured. The same article closes with 'For more control over the self-registration process, edit the CommmunitiesSelfRegController' (Salesforce's own spelling, with three m's), which is option A and where profile and account assignment logic belongs; the parent article agrees that you can 'completely customize the self-registration process by modifying the Apex controller'. Option C is invented — there is no SelfRegistration trigger. Option D is the near-miss: you edit the controller but you configure the *page*, so the controller is not itself a setting in Login & Registration.

Key A confirmed against the flow's stated purpose and shape. 'To integrate apps that run on devices with limited input or display capabilities, such as Smart TVs, appliances, and other IoT devices, use the OAuth 2.0 device flow. Users can connect these apps to Salesforce by accessing a browser on a device with more advanced input capabilities' — a fitness tracker is that device, and the community on a phone or desktop is the richer browser. The article's worked example is the same pattern: the device gets a user code and verification URL, the user enters the code in a browser and authorises, and the device polls the token endpoint. Named Credentials (B) authenticate Salesforce's own outbound callouts, SSO Settings (C) configure inbound federation, and Login Flows (D) run after an existing authentication — none of them pair a device to a user account.

Key A,B,D confirmed, and the distractor is provably misplaced rather than merely unlikely. The web server flow article matches the stem's grant type outright — 'the OAuth 2.0 web server flow, which implements the OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant type' — and grounds option A in one sentence: 'the server hosting the web app must be able to protect the external client app's identity, defined by the client ID and client secret.' Scopes and access tokens are both documented there too. Option C is the give-away: the phrase 'verification URL' never appears on the web server flow page, while the device flow page states that Salesforce 'returns a human-readable user code, verification URL, and device code'. Verification URL therefore belongs to the device flow, exactly as the deck's explanation claims.

Key C,D confirmed against the documented definition of the service provider role: Salesforce is configured 'as a service provider' precisely in the configuration where 'your users can log in to Salesforce with credentials from an external identity provider'. That is this scenario — the customer is trying to reach the Salesforce-hosted Customer Community, so Salesforce is the SP in every option, and whichever external service authenticates the user is the IdP. Facebook and Google are therefore the identity providers, giving C and D. A inverts the pair, and B is a relationship between two external services that plays no part in a login to Salesforce. Mechanically social sign-on runs through an Auth Provider rather than SAML, but the SP/IdP role assignment is identical.

Key D confirmed, and the documented definition of the SP role is what rules out the tempting answer. Salesforce is a service provider in the configuration where 'your users can log in to Salesforce with credentials from an external identity provider' — but in this scenario no user ever logs in to Salesforce. The stem is explicit that UC avoids provisioning users in Salesforce and integrates the portal's ideas through the API, so the SiteMinder/Active Directory SSO authenticates employees to the portal only. Salesforce therefore sits outside the SSO topology, which is D. Option C is the trap: being the application that stores the data does not make an org a service provider; the SP role is defined by the authentication flow, not by where the records live. A server-to-server API call authenticates a single integration identity and is not SSO at all, which also disposes of A and B.

Key C confirmed, and the two rejected options fail for a documented reason rather than by elimination. Custom Login Flows names this exact use: 'After Salesforce authenticates a user, the login flow directs the user through a process, such as enforcing strong authentication' — so a flow is the supported place to make a challenge conditional. Option D fails because it conflates two mechanisms: org Trusted IP Ranges specify addresses 'from which users can log in without receiving an identity verification challenge', which is device activation, and that article never mentions MFA or two-factor at all; there is no 'Login Range list under 2FA Setup'. Option B fails because the Two-Factor Authentication for User Interface Logins permission applies unconditionally, so it cannot be network-dependent, and profile Login IP Ranges deny logins outright rather than adding a challenge.

Key D confirmed on the two discriminators the item is built from. Custom vs standard: Active Directory group membership is not a standard SAML claim, so it has to arrive as a custom attribute, which eliminates A and C. Handler vs login flow: JIT provisioning is documented as the hook that consumes the assertion — 'an identity provider passes user information to Salesforce in a SAML 2.0 assertion, which is processed by an Apex JIT handler class. The JIT handler does the heavy lifting of creating and updating user accounts' — and because the handler is Apex it can perform PermissionSetAssignment DML, with updateUser firing on subsequent logins so group changes keep tracking. Stated honestly: the article does not itself use the words 'permission set', so it supports the mechanism and the hook rather than that specific assignment; the permission-set capability follows from the handler being Apex.

Key B,D,E confirmed, with B documented in one sentence: 'Specifying a Start URL makes the application available in the app menu and in App Launcher.' D matches the same article's instruction to configure the external app as a connected app with Salesforce defined as its SAML identity provider, and E matches Enable Salesforce as a SAML Identity Provider. Auth Providers (C) handle inbound SSO where Salesforce is the service provider, the opposite direction; Identity Connect (A) is AD synchronisation. One nuance recorded for future passes rather than changed here: the current Enable Salesforce as a SAML Identity Provider article lists only a certificate and the Enable button as prerequisites and never mentions My Domain, so E's 'with My Domain' is no longer a distinct step — My Domain is now universal for orgs rather than an SSO-specific prerequisite.

Key A,B confirmed from a single article. It walks exactly this scenario — an external web app that authenticates with SAML, configured as a connected app with the Salesforce org as its SAML identity provider — which is option B. And option A follows from 'Specifying a Start URL makes the application available in the app menu and in App Launcher', which is precisely how the billing app becomes launchable from inside Salesforce. Canvas (C) is correctly rejected: the same article says to skip the Start URL field for a canvas app because Canvas embeds an app rather than redirecting to it, and the stem states a redirect is acceptable. Identity Connect (D) is AD sync and unrelated.

Key D confirmed, and the documentation supplies the exact policy that produces this symptom. A connected app's Refresh Token Policy offers 'Expire refresh token after n', described as 'valid for a fixed amount of time' — a fixed clock started at first authorisation, which is why the complaint tracks the initial-launch cohort specifically rather than all users. The default is 'Refresh token is valid until revoked', so an org seeing timed re-auth has deliberately moved off it. Worth naming the trap: the stem's mention of a changed URI Scheme makes option A look urgent, but the refresh_token grant is a token-endpoint exchange that does not use the callback URL, and a broken callback would fail every user rather than one cohort.

Key A confirmed, with the documentation matching the once-a-day symptom almost word for word. 'Expire refresh token after n—The refresh token is valid for a fixed amount of time. For example, if the policy states one day, the user can obtain new sessions only for 24 hours.' The inactivity variant, 'Expire refresh token if not used for n', would not fire for a daily-active user, so a daily prompt points at the fixed-period setting. The fix is the default, 'Refresh token is valid until revoked'. Option B is ruled out because the policy 'is evaluated only during usage of the issued refresh token' rather than by request volume.

Key A confirmed on two counts, both read off the article rather than inferred. The target system matches: the page's own worked scenario is 'user provisioning for a G Suite connected app', where creating a user provisions them in G Suite and deactivating them deprovisions them. And the operation set matches exactly what the stem asks for — its event table maps Create user -> Create, Enable user -> Activate, Disable user -> Deactivate, Freeze user -> Freeze, Unfreeze user -> Unfreeze, Reactivate user -> Reactivate. That covers enable, freeze/suspend, disable and reactivate declaratively, so the JIT handler (B), polling endpoint (C) and trigger (D) are all unnecessary custom work.

Key D confirmed almost verbatim. Salesforce Identity Licenses states: 'Purchase the Identity Only license when you need extra licenses for employees to access only identity services, such as single sign-on (SSO)', and its worked example is employees who 'don't need access to all the solutions included with a Salesforce license' but must 'sign in to a custom Your Benefits web app directly from your Salesforce org using SSO' — the stem's custom time-tracking app in different words. The same page enumerates the other two options and rules them out: External Identity is the license for external users, and Identity Verification Credits is the SMS add-on, not an access license. Identity Connect is a separate AD-sync product, not a user license.

Re-verified rather than re-litigated. This question was moved A->B on 2026-08-09 and carries the only correction stamp in the deck; that reasoning still holds and no new evidence contradicts it, so it is confirmed as-is and the existing stamp is deliberately left intact. Recorded here so the pass has a verdict for every question rather than a silent gap. The settled fact behind it: an Authentication Provider federates over OpenID Connect or custom OAuth 2.0 and has no LDAP capability, while Delegated Authentication is the feature that validates credentials against LDAP — so option A described something not configurable.

findings.explanation:
Dynamic branding turns on one documented mechanism: the Experience ID. You extend the identity endpoints with an expid value — site-url/services/oauth2/authorize/expid_value and site-url/idp/endpoint/HttpPost/expid_value — or pass expid={value} on the login page, CommunitiesSelfReg, and forgot-password URLs, and Salesforce resolves the brand-specific logo and content from that value at run time. That is option C.
The other half is that the site must be one you can brand in Experience Builder. Every Experience Cloud template except Salesforce Tabs + Visualforce is a Lightning template customised in Experience Builder, and each one 'comes with its own set of pages for login, identity verification, password resets, and self-registration'. So option D is the one template that rules dynamic branding out, and an external CMS (B) is nowhere required — a CMS URL is merely one place the {expid} placeholder can point.
Be aware that option A is narrower than the documentation: nothing restricts dynamic branding to the Customer Account Portal template specifically. Read A as 'a Lightning/Experience Builder template, of which Customer Account Portal is one' — that is the claim the docs support.
findings.note: Key A,C stands as the best-supported pair, but the item is partly defective and the explanation now says so. Option C is solidly documented. Option A is not: 'Brand Your Experience Builder Pages' never mentions the Customer Account Portal template at all, and states that *each* Experience Cloud template ships its own login/verification/reset/self-registration pages. The real requirement is an Experience Builder (Lightning) template — which is why option D, Salesforce Tabs + Visualforce, is the genuine exclusion. A is defensible only on the loose reading 'a Lightning template such as Customer Account Portal'; flagged rather than silently confirmed.

Key D confirmed. The Experience ID is the documented mechanism for varying the login experience per brand within a single site: supported identity endpoints are extended with an expid value, including the OAuth authorize endpoint and both SAML IdP endpoints, and the value selects the branding at run time. That is what scales to 150+ sub-brands without 150 sites (A) or 150 orgs (B). Option C is the near-miss worth naming: Audiences is a real Experience Builder feature for varying page content, but the parameter carried through the OAuth and SAML flows is expid, not an 'audience ID'.

Key B confirmed, and the existing citation was rendered and is on point rather than merely plausible. The article opens 'To integrate IoT devices with the Salesforce API, use the OAuth 2.0 asset token flow' and describes tokens that allow 'registration of device data with the Salesforce platform and linking the device to Salesforce CRM data about the customer, account, or contact' — which is precisely the sensor-data-plus-maintenance model in the stem. Also checked for retirement, since a device flow was removed from the default Salesforce CLI connected app in Aug 2025: the asset token flow itself is current.

Key B stands and the existing explanation is substantively right, but its only citation (SMS Identity Verification) never uses the word 'credit', so it did not support the claim it was attached to. The Identity Verification Credits Add-On License article settles it: the licence 'typically includes 25,000 SMS messages per month, 300,000 credits per year', i.e. credits are denominated in SMS sends. That confirms B and rules out A (no per-community 10,000 monthly allowance) and D (not scaled to community licence counts).
